lead: A perfectly round fiber would carry the two polarization modes at the same speed. Real fiber is slightly elliptical and stressed, so its refractive index differs along two transverse axes. That difference is birefringence. The two polarization modes then arrive at slightly different times, and the delay is polarization mode dispersion (PMD). Along a cabled link the axes twist at random, so the delay grows as the square root of length, not linearly. PMD matters at 10 Gbit/s and above, and in coherent systems it still limits reach.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for modes and polarization, and chapter 2.6 for group delay differences.

blocks.text: Drawing and cabling leave the core slightly elliptical, and they add stress that is not the same in all directions. The refractive index is then not one number: it is n_x along one transverse axis and n_y along the other. The difference B = |n_x − n_y| is the birefringence. The two polarization modes see different indices, so they have different propagation constants and different group delays. In a short, uniform piece of fiber the differential group delay (DGD) grows linearly with length, as the formula below shows. A round, stress-free fiber has B = 0, and the two modes travel together. The axes are called the principal axes. Birefringence is tiny in good fiber, but it is never exactly zero. Most links ignore it below 10 Gbit/s. The delay is small in a short jumper but can matter over hundreds of kilometres.

blocks.where: Δτ is the DGD in ps; β₁ₓ and β₁ᵧ are group delays per unit length in ps/km; L is the fiber length in km.

sections.h3: Random axes give a square-root law

blocks.text: In a real cable the elliptical axes do not stay fixed. Bending, twisting and temperature rotate them along the length. The delay therefore does not add as L; it adds like a random walk, because each short section adds a small delay with a random sign. The mean DGD follows the first formula below. Modern fiber has D_PMD about 0.05 to 0.2 ps/√km; older cable can exceed 1 ps/√km. At 100 km with 0.1 ps/√km the mean is 1 ps, not 10 ps. The instantaneous DGD follows a Maxwellian distribution. Most values sit below the mean, but rare values near three times the mean cause outages. Keep the mean below about 10% of the bit period, as the second formula states. This is why PMD is often a 40 Gbit/s problem.

blocks.where: ⟨Δτ⟩ is the mean DGD in ps; D_PMD is the PMD coefficient in ps/√km; L is the length in km.
D_PMD is the PMD coefficient in ps/√km; L is the length in km; T_b is the bit period in ps; R_b is the bit rate in Gbit/s, with T_b = 1000/R_b. Both sides are in ps.

figure.caption: Mean DGD against length for D_PMD = 0.1 ps/√km, the same coefficient as the worked example. The curve rises as √L; at 100 km it gives 1 ps.

spec.aria: A curve of mean differential group delay against length that rises as the square root of length, not as a straight line.

examples.question: A 400 km link uses fiber with D_PMD = 0.1 ps/√km. (a) Find the mean DGD. (b) Compare it with the bit period at 10 Gbit/s and 40 Gbit/s, using 10% of the bit period as the limit. (c) Comment on the Maxwellian tail.
steps: At 10 Gbit/s, T_b = 100 ps and the limit is 0.1 × 100 = 10 ps. The mean 2 ps is comfortable.
At 40 Gbit/s, T_b = 25 ps and the limit is 2.5 ps. The mean 2 ps is close to it.
The Maxwellian tail reaches about 3 × 2 = 6 ps, which exceeds 2.5 ps, so errors are possible at 40 Gbit/s.
examples.answer: Mean DGD = 2 ps; it is safe at 10 Gbit/s and marginal at 40 Gbit/s because the tail exceeds the 2.5 ps limit.
examples.check:
import math
L = 400
D = 0.1
mean = D * math.sqrt(L)
print(mean)
tb10 = 1000 / 10
print(tb10)
print(0.1 * tb10)
tb40 = 1000 / 40
print(tb40)
print(0.1 * tb40)
print(3 * mean)

traps: Using Δτ proportional to L. A real cable gives D_PMD √L; linear growth belongs to a short, uniform fiber.
Writing D_PMD in ps/km or dropping the square root. Its unit is ps/√km.
Treating the mean DGD as the whole story. The Maxwellian tail reaches about three times the mean.
Comparing mean DGD with the bit period instead of 10% of it.
Confusing PMD with chromatic dispersion: both spread pulses, but chromatic dispersion scales as L and comes from wavelength, while PMD scales as √L and comes from polarization.

quiz.a: B = |n_x − n_y|, the refractive-index difference between the two transverse axes.

quiz.q: Why does mean DGD scale as √L in a cabled link?
quiz.a: The principal axes rotate randomly, so short-section delays add like a random walk; variance grows with L.

quiz.q: D_PMD = 0.2 ps/√km and L = 900 km. Find the mean DGD.
At 10 Gbit/s, mean DGD = 4 ps. Check the 10% rule and the 3× tail.
quiz.a: T_b = 100 ps, limit 10 ps. Mean passes; tail 12 ps exceeds the limit, so outages are possible.

quiz.q: Why is PMD more serious at 40 Gbit/s than at 10 Gbit/s?
quiz.a: Bit period falls from 100 ps to 25 ps, so the 10% limit falls from 10 ps to 2.5 ps while DGD is unchanged.

quiz.q: A 40 Gbit/s link must keep mean DGD ≤ 2.5 ps. With D_PMD = 0.1 ps/√km, find maximum L.
A link passes the mean-DGD rule but still shows burst errors. Give one PMD-related reason.
quiz.a: The instantaneous DGD follows a Maxwellian tail; a rare value near 3× the mean exceeds the limit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Coherent receivers at 100 Gbit/s and above track polarization continuously, so they tolerate much larger PMD than direct-detection links. Product data sheets still quote a PMD coefficient, and installed older cable is measured before an upgrade. Researchers study polarization-mode dispersion and polarization-dependent loss together, because both distort the state of polarization. Search for “PMD coefficient”, “Maxwellian DGD distribution” and “polarization tracking coherent receiver”.
